summary:
TerraHydro is a geospatial decision-support platform designed to protect Saudi Arabia’s non-renewable groundwater reserves amid rapid urban and industrial expansion. Using NASA’s GLDAS 2.2 Catchment dataset—which assimilates GRACE satellite observations, we analyzed 11 years of weekly groundwater storage data (2015–2025) across 152 Saudi cities.

At its core, the Groundwater Explorer visualizes historical storage trends and spatial heatmaps, powering two strategic modules: the AI Data Center Recommender, which models aquifer depletion lifetimes to guide sustainable siting, and the Desalination Priority Recommender, which helps governments identify which cities need urgent prioritization for desalination investments based on water decline.

Looking ahead, curating higher-resolution, neighborhood-scale groundwater measurements will unlock broader public and commercial impact—empowering homebuyers to assess water security before purchasing property, guiding contractors to build residential developments where water is sustainable, and helping desalination providers focus their infrastructure campaigns. Ultimately, making localized groundwater risks transparent fosters widespread public awareness and responsible water stewardship in arid regions.
details:
What Does It Do & How Does It Work?

TerraHydro turns 11 years of satellite groundwater data (2015–2025) into practical planning insights for 152 municipalities across all 13 provinces in Saudi Arabia. Instead of just displaying raw environmental numbers, the platform helps planners and engineers see how much groundwater a city actually has before committing to major infrastructure.

We built the platform around a single data pipeline and three main tools:

  • Data Pipeline & Unit Conversion: We take weekly (7-day) observations from NASA’s GLDAS 2.2 Catchment dataset (which integrates GRACE gravimetry data) and combine them with each city’s urban footprint area (km²), coordinates, and data-quality flags. Since satellite readings come in water-equivalent thickness (mm or L/m²), the system multiplies those values by each municipality's area to estimate actual water volume in Liters, m³, GL, and TL.
  • Groundwater Explorer (Main Hub): This is where users explore the dataset. You can filter by province, compare different cities side-by-side, and scrub through any week between 2015 and 2025. It also renders a groundwater storage heatmap clipped to Saudi Arabia's borders and calculates 11-year averages, storage ranges, and overall net changes.
  • AI Data Center Recommender: AI data centers require massive amounts of water for cooling. This tool takes a city's groundwater volume on any chosen date and weighs it against projected annual cooling demand to estimate how many years the local aquifer could sustain the facility, ranking the safest locations for new builds.
  • Desalination Priority Recommender: By running linear regression across the 11-year timeline, this tool flags municipalities experiencing the steepest long-term groundwater drops, helping identify where new desalination capacity or pipeline expansions are needed most urgently.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Smarter Data Center Placement: Helps tech companies and infrastructure planners avoid building water-heavy AI data centers over depleting aquifers.
    • Homebuyers can check long-term water security in an area before buying a house.
    • Real estate developers and contractors can plan housing projects in locations with reliable water reserves.
    • Desalination providers can direct supply and distribution efforts to regions with the largest deficits.
    • Local residents can easily see and understand underground water trends that are normally invisible to the public.

Tools, Coding Languages & Software Used

  • Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript (ESNext), HTML5, CSS3.
  • Frontend & UI: React 19, React Router (HashRouter), Tailwind CSS, and Lucide React icons.
  • Mapping & Spatial Rendering: Leaflet, React-Leaflet, a custom HTML5 Canvas interpolation layer (GroundwaterHeatLayer) masked to Saudi Arabia's border polygon (saudiBoundary.ts), and CARTO basemaps (Voyager and Dark Matter).
  • Charts & Visualization: Recharts for multi-city historical comparisons, linear regression trendlines, and aquifer depletion projections.
  • Build & Testing: Vite (with Rolldown), Vitest (36 unit and dataset integration tests covering regression math, unit conversions, and heatmap interpolation), and Oxlint.
  • Deployment: We ran build and test scripts locally before pushing production releases manually via the Cloudflare API, rather than relying on automated Git push pipelines.
  • Earth Observation Data: NASA GLDAS-2.2 Catchment Land Surface Model (assimilating GRACE/GRACE-FO water storage anomalies) at 7-day intervals from 2015 to 2025.

How Is the Project Creative?

  1. Connecting Space Hydrology to AI Infrastructure: Most groundwater tools stop at showing historical charts. We took NASA's satellite water data and applied it directly to a real, urgent problem in the Middle East: figuring out where to build AI data centers without draining non-renewable desert aquifers.
  2. Custom Border-Clipped Heatmap: Because satellite grid points are spaced apart, raw data looks patchy on a city map. We wrote our own client-side interpolation layer (GroundwaterHeatLayer.tsx) in HTML5 Canvas that generates a smooth groundwater surface and clips it cleanly to Saudi Arabia’s exact borders.
  3. Practical Volume Estimates: Raw satellite metrics like millimeters of water equivalent are hard to picture in city planning. By scaling those readings against each municipality's actual land area, the app translates abstract hydrology into concrete volumes (m³, Gigaliters, and Teroliters).

What Factors Did Our Team Consider?

  • Regional Differences Across Saudi Arabia: Saudi Arabia depends on both deep, non-renewable fossil aquifers and coastal desalination, and water stress varies widely by region. We structured the app around all 13 administrative provinces so cities are evaluated in their proper geographic context.
  • Being Honest About Data Limits: Satellite gravimetry has coarse spatial resolution and isn't exact down to a single street. To keep users from over-interpreting the numbers, we added a Data Quality Badge (High Quality vs. Local Grid Only) and an interactive Methodology Modal explaining how the estimates work and where their limits lie.
  • Testing Across Different Timeframes: Water reserves shift over seasons and droughts. Instead of locking the analysis to a single recent snapshot, we built a shared date selector (DatasetContext and ObservationDatePicker) so users can run scenarios against any historical week from 2015 to 2025.
  • Fast Browser Performance: Rather than setting up a heavy backend database, we pre-processed the 11-year dataset for all 152 cities and used memoized client-side calculations. Filtering, timeline playback, and chart updates happen instantly in the browser.

AI / Super Intelligence (SI) Disclosure

We used AI tools (Google Gemini and AI coding assistants) during the hackathon to brainstorm ideas, write and debug code, refine SVG styling (BrandLogo), generate unit tests, and edit our project documentation. All groundwater and hydrological data comes directly from NASA's GLDAS-2.2 / GRACE Earth observation datasets.
